messages.subject: invariance testing with categorical data and multiple imputation
parts:
Hello all, 

I am trying to carry on invariance test in a dataset that contains ordered variables with some missing data. I am using "DWLS" estimator, and I have used multiple imputation (mice) and everything is fine until I run the compareFit() function. When I run that function, in order to obtain the tipical "Chi-Squared Difference Test"   I obtain a nested model comparison with the F statistic... 

It is obvious I am missing something... can anyone please help me out?

Thank you,

messages.author: b8fd92e5e3662745
messages.subject: Re: invariance testing with categorical data and multiple imputation
parts:
Multiple imputation leaves behind a finite degrees of freedom to go into t-tests of individual coefficients and F-tests for multiple coefficients (including model as a whole). Best check with van Buuren's FIMD book https://stefvanbuuren.name/fimd/sec-whyandwhen.html#sec:df -- if you have not read that book, you arguably should not be embarking on multiple imputation projects. The degrees of freedom increase with the number of imputations, and in the worst case it is as low as [# imputations]-1 for the entirely made up data. Historically the magic number of 5 imputations was used for most imputation problems... but then the 1970 estimation problems when Rubin first published this stuff were "estimate regression with five predictors on data set of size n=70", and for those problems 5 imputations would produce 50 degrees of freedom which was OK. Degrees of freedom is a very helpful first step diagnostics that your imputations make any sense. (The subsequent diagnostic steps would include checking distributions -- see https://stefvanbuuren.name/fimd/ch-practice.html, https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/pdf/10.1177/1536867X1201200301, https://doi.org/10.1002/sim.6926.) For SEM models, I would run enough imputations that the imputation degrees of freedom exceed the sample size and exceed twice the model degrees of freedom.
